title: Carbon Dioxide Around the Globe, Early 2020, on a world map

source.visualizer: AJ Christensen (SSAI), Greg Shirah (NASA/GSFC), Helen-Nicole Kostis (USRA), Mark SubbaRao (NASA/GSFC)
source.dataset: DYAMOND, the experimental coupled GEOS-MITgcm model (NASA GEOS)

frames.label: 14 January to 3 March 2020
frames.alt: World map of carbon dioxide from NASA's film, 14 January to 3 March 2020: a dark Earth with orange and red where carbon dioxide is dense, brightest over eastern China, with fires across central Africa and South America and a faint tan haze over the northern hemisphere. The far north and south are dim grey: the film never showed them face-on.
frames.about: NASA's turning globe flattened into one map. Each place shows its carbon dioxide in the weeks it faced the camera: East Asia in January, Africa in February, the Americas in early March.

legend.summary: A slow scan line moves west to east across a world map of carbon dioxide, made from NASA's film of the globe turning, 14 January to 3 March 2020.
legend.method: Only what is under the scan line plays. A note rings where the line crosses dense carbon dioxide: north rings higher and in your left ear, south lower and in your right ear. A deep hum follows all the carbon dioxide under the line.

items.meaning: Dense carbon dioxide crossing the line, from fires, cities and industry. Louder = denser.
All the carbon dioxide under the line: quiet over clean air, fuller over plumes.

legend.caveat: NASA's colour key has no numbers, so levels are relative: faint tan is the least carbon dioxide shown, red the most. Each place is averaged over the weeks it faced the camera, so East Asia is from January and the Americas from early March.
